records.name: Jēkabs
records.evidence_locations: Siliņš 1990 printed p177 (PDF180), exact headword Jēkabs, folklore note; text layer read.
records.facts_used: Jēkabs is the Latvian form of Jacob (Jākobs), the name of the Old Testament patriarch and of two apostles. In Latvian folk custom new bread was baked on Jēkabs’ day, 25 July, and the first loaf was carried to the field as an offering. The name is recorded in Rūjiena in 1610 and has been in Latvian calendars since 1817.

records.name: Jakob
records.evidence_locations: Rajandi PDF85/printed87, Jakob(us) entry listing Jaak, Jako, Jaagup, Jass (text layer); Mägiste 1929 PDF34–35; Mägiste 1936 PDF39.
records.facts_used: Jakob is one of the Estonian forms of Jacob, from the Hebrew Ya‘aqov, explained as ‘the one who holds the heel’ or ‘the one who supplants’. Its medieval spread rested on the veneration of the apostle James. The old Estonian farming calendar said on Jaagup’s day, 25 July: “Scythe on the peg, sickle in hand!”, and the weather lore added: “Before Jaak, pray for rain; after it, it comes by itself.” As early as 1217 the son of Kaupo is recorded as Jacobi, and from the 15th century the name was moderately common among Estonians; Jaakson and Jakobson are very common surnames.
